summary: Arabic has a near and a far demonstrative, each with a masculine, a feminine and a plural for people: هٰذَا / هٰذِهِ / هٰؤُلَاءِ “this, these” and ذٰلِكَ / تِلْكَ / أُولٰئِكَ “that, those”; هُنَا is “here”, هُنَاكَ “there”. They agree with the noun — and plurals of things take the feminine singular: هٰذِهِ الْكُتُبُ (these books). The article decides between a sentence and a phrase: هٰذَا طَالِبٌ = this is a student; هٰذَا الطَّالِبُ = this student.

head: near — this, these
far — that, those
rows: feminine singular — also things in the plural

items.title: هٰذَا طَالِبٌ — a sentence
points: no article on the noun, tanwīn (-un)

items.title: هٰذَا الطَّالِبُ … — a phrase
points: it needs a predicate: هٰذَا الطَّالِبُ هُنَا (this student is here)

blocks.title: Agreement.
blocks.text: هٰذَا رَجُلٌ (m.) — هٰذِهِ بِنْتٌ (f.) — هٰؤُلَاءِ طُلَّابٌ (people) — هٰذِهِ كُتُبٌ (things in the plural → feminine singular).

blocks.title: “This is THE …”.
blocks.text: For “this is the student” put a pronoun between: هٰذَا هُوَ الطَّالِبُ. Without it, هٰذَا الطَّالِبُ is only “this student”.

blocks.title: Two of them.
blocks.text: For two people or things there are dual demonstratives, هٰذَانِ (m.) and هَاتَانِ (f.) “these two” — they come with the dual in lesson 5.
هُنَاكَ also means “there is / there are”: هُنَاكَ طُلَّابٌ = there are students (there).

askYourself: Is the noun masculine or feminine? (ة usually means feminine)
Plural? People → هٰؤُلَاءِ / أُولٰئِكَ; things → هٰذِهِ / تِلْكَ.
Do I mean “this is a …” (no article on the noun) or “this … is …” (article on the noun, then a predicate)?
“This is THE …”? → put هُوَ / هِيَ / هُمْ in between.

traps: *هٰؤُلَاءِ الْكُتُبُ is wrong: things in the plural take هٰذِهِ.
هٰذَا الْكِتَابُ is not a sentence; هٰذَا كِتَابٌ is.
The ā of هٰذَا and ذٰلِكَ is a small (dagger) alif: unvocalized هذا، ذلك — no long alif.
The feminine of ذٰلِكَ is تِلْكَ, a different word.

quiz.why: Feminine noun → هٰذِهِ; no article → a sentence.
Things in the plural take the feminine singular.
People in the plural, far → أُولٰئِكَ.
With the article it is a phrase; “this is the student” = هٰذَا هُوَ الطَّالِبُ.

seeAlso.note: Hebrew puts the demonstrative after the noun, both with the article — הַבַּיִת הַזֶּה “the house the this” — where Arabic puts it first: هٰذَا الْبَيْتُ. Arabic ذ corresponds to Hebrew ז (זֶה ↔ ذَا).
German dieser / diese / dieses is declined in four cases; for “this is a …” the invariable das ist … works like هٰذَا ….
Chinese 这 / 那 never change for gender or number but need a measure word before the noun (这本书).

notes.text: Greek also puts the article after the demonstrative — αυτό το σπίτι, “this the house” — like هٰذَا الْبَيْتُ; and αυτό είναι σπίτι (this is a house) has no article, like هٰذَا بَيْتٌ.
Hungarian ez a ház (“this the house”) is built exactly like هٰذَا الْبَيْتُ.
Russian это in “this is …” never changes (это книга); Arabic هٰذَا / هٰذِهِ agrees with the noun: هٰذَا كِتَابٌ, هٰذِهِ غُرْفَةٌ.
Spanish has three distances (este, ese, aquel); Arabic has two: هٰذَا near, ذٰلِكَ far.
English this / these change only for number; Arabic also for gender (هٰذَا / هٰذِهِ), and things in the plural take the feminine singular: هٰذِهِ الْكُتُبُ (these books).
French ce / cette agree in gender like هٰذَا / هٰذِهِ — but for things in the plural Arabic uses the feminine singular: هٰذِهِ الْكُتُبُ (ces livres).
Hindi यह / वह do not change for gender; Arabic هٰذَا / هٰذِهِ do.
Persian این / آن never change (این کتاب‌ها, these books); Arabic switches between هٰذَا, هٰذِهِ and هٰؤُلَاءِ.
Marathi हा / ही / हे agree with the noun’s gender like هٰذَا / هٰذِهِ — Marathi with a neuter as well.
Turkish has three demonstratives (bu, şu, o) that never change; Arabic has two distances that agree in gender and number.
Japanese has three distances (これ / それ / あれ) and no agreement; Arabic has two (هٰذَا, ذٰلِكَ) that agree.
Finnish tämä / tuo / se are three and take case endings; Arabic has two, and they agree in gender instead.
Swahili demonstratives follow the noun and agree by class (kitabu hiki, vitabu hivi); Arabic ones come first and agree by gender: هٰذَا الْكِتَابُ.
Luganda demonstratives follow the noun and agree by class (ekitabo kino, this book); Arabic puts هٰذَا first.
Vietnamese puts the demonstrative after the noun, with a classifier (quyển sách này, this book); Arabic puts it first, with the article on the noun: هٰذَا الْكِتَابُ.
Inuktitut has many demonstratives that also say where the thing is — above, below, inside, outside; Arabic has just two distances.
